BREAKING: The US goods trade deficit widened by -$17.4 billion, or -17%, in July, to -$118.8 billion, the largest gap since March 2025.

US goods imports rose +$11.4 billion, or +4%, to $318.2 billion, their highest level since March 2025.

Capital goods imports, which include computers and accessories, semiconductors and telecommunications equipment, surged +11%, their largest monthly increase since 1993.

At the same time, exports fell -$6.0 billion, or -3%, to $199.4 billion, their lowest since January, driven by a -11% decline in exports of industrial goods.

Excluding the 4 months between December 2024 and March 2025, when companies accelerated imports ahead of anticipated US tariff increases, July’s goods trade deficit was the largest on record.

The trade gap is widening again.

BREAKING: The US government is now running a primary budget deficit of -3.59% of GDP, the largest among major advanced economies.

The primary budget deficit EXCLUDES the $1.1+ trillion in interest payments on existing government debt.

This is followed by the UK at -3.51% of the country’s GDP.

Belgium, France, Austria, and the Euro Area run primary budget deficits of -2.14%, -1.97%, -1.66%, and -1.40%, respectively.

In other words, even excluding the cost of servicing existing debt, which is the 2nd-largest US government expenditure, even larger than defense spending, the US deficit is the biggest relative to GDP among all major advanced economies.

US deficit spending is out of control.

My view is that the "cancer" spread due to fiscal and can be traced back to the covid fiscal response + subsequent pro-cyclical deficit spending. The "man on the street" is not mad b/c cpi is currently  >2%...He's mad b/c the house that costs $250k in his mind is now $600k and the cost to finance it is ~7% not 4%. The world changed over night. The anger is rooted in this change.

Wrt current Fed policy, they are restricting the areas that matter to the general public. To hike enough to slow the AI buildout would require - almost by definition - sacrificing the labor side of the dual mandate. The only thing worse than an inflation shock (which is really behind us now) is an inflation shock followed by a recession/market crash. Not to mention the fact that the rise in oil price is supply-induced and constitutes a tightening (i.e. not something the Fed should respond to).

With that said, the AI build out is meaningful and has/is shifting the "neutral" rate higher. I think that (along w/ H1 fiscal stim) is what steepened the yield curve and signaled that maybe 3.75% is roughly neutral. Tough environment for monetary authorities but holding here seems wise.

Just my rambling 2cents fwiw
